summary:
Arturo Nunez, drawing on nearly ten years at Unity, introduces Nereu, a browser-based game-building tool representing a next-generation game engine with no manual. He opens with a demo in which a user with no coding or 3D modeling experience describes wanting a WASD-controlled animated robot, buildings, rain, and a follow camera. The assistant, named Bibi, handles each request by selecting relevant assets and configuring them, using the vocabulary tutorials already teach, such as 'press A to jump, press A again in the air.'

Arturo argues that powerful traditional engines paired with LLMs still place context on the engine's vocabulary rather than the game's. Controlling a character requires a mesh, renderer, animator, rigid body, collider, audio source, and movement logic, nearly all identical boilerplate across games. Nereu inverts this: every entity is an asset with intent tags like character, animated, or double jump. Systems query by tag, so anything tagged vehicle, player, and drivable is moved, enabling a building tagged drivable to be dropped into a Mario Kart-style race.

Arturo describes how context is assembled for the assistant, combining scene data with extra information like asset types and the user's stated game style. Vision models were used to pre-tag roughly six to seven thousand assets because manual tagging was infeasible. The assistant only adds or removes tags rather than executing arbitrary scripts, though JavaScript extension is available. To keep context small, he borrows level-of-detail from rendering: nearby assets receive full tag values and settings, while distant ones collapse to a position and type, with grass simply omitted. He closes by positioning the assistant as an unsticker rather than a one-shot game generator, distinguishing Nereu from world-model-based game generation, which he sees as a different medium with unsolved real-time physics and rendering challenges. The tool is in closed alpha.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Demo: building a game live by describing it
sections.summary: Arturo opens with a live-style demo showing how a user with no coding or 3D modeling experience can describe what they want in plain language and have the Bibi assistant assemble a small game: a WASD-controlled animated robot, a selection of buildings, rain, and a follow camera, all added through conversational prompts.

sections.title: Why making games is hard
sections.summary: Arturo explains the wide skill set required to make games, programming, 3D modeling, rendering, music, animation, and the difficulty of finding one person strong across all of them. He notes that game-making should be a creative outlet and fun, not just a commercial grind, and argues non-professionals should be able to build games just as non-programmers can now write code with AI.

sections.title: Ten years at Unity watching the same struggles repeat
sections.summary: Reflecting on his Unity tenure, Arturo describes watching thousands of developers wrestle with the same boilerplate, which motivated him to leave and eventually build Nereu, after stints at MongoDB and an asset-versioning startup.

sections.title: Powerful engines and LLMs that still do not compose
sections.summary: Even with powerful engines and LLMs, building a bridge between code/engineering vocabulary and game design vocabulary is suboptimal, causing models to reinvent wheels like follow cameras on every request.

sections.title: The boilerplate behind controlling a character
sections.summary: Arturo enumerates the standard character stack in a traditional engine (mesh, renderer, animator, rigid body, collider, audio source, movement logic) and argues most of it is identical boilerplate that developers must still configure by reading component docs and slider descriptions.

sections.title: Everything is an asset, and tags describe intent
sections.summary: He proposes flipping the model so every entity is an asset with intent tags such as character, animated, or double jump, using the same language tutorials already use. Systems then query by tag, so anything tagged vehicle, player, and drivable is moved, allowing a building to be tagged drivable and used in a Mario Kart-style race.

sections.title: The asset tag system, and tagging a building as drivable
sections.summary: Arturo names the approach the Asset Tag System, grounded in ECS and data-oriented design, and reiterates the building-as-drivable example as evidence that tags, not archetypes, drive behavior.

sections.title: How the prompt gets its context
sections.summary: He walks through context assembly for the assistant: scene data plus extra context like asset types and the user's described game style, with the assistant only adding or removing tags rather than executing arbitrary scripts. JavaScript extension is available, but intentionally absent by default. He closes by noting the hardest part is composing tags and systems across genres, post-processing, and mood, and that the tool is in closed alpha.

sections.title: Level of detail, applied to context assembly
sections.summary: Arturo explains why the whole scene cannot be fed to the LLM (a 100-asset scene with most being ignorable grass) and introduces level-of-detail from rendering as the solution: nearby assets get full tag values and settings, distant ones collapse to a position and type, and irrelevant assets are omitted, with context updating as the user moves and edits.

sections.title: Vision models used to pre-tag the asset library
sections.summary: He notes that vision models were used to tag roughly six to seven thousand assets, since the assets only arrived with names and 3D files and manual tagging was infeasible.

sections.title: Getting unstuck rather than one-shotting a game
sections.summary: Arturo closes the main pitch by positioning Bibi as an unsticker that helps users learn the language of game design rather than one-shotting games nobody will play. He notes users have reported understanding programming concepts along the way, which was not the initial goal.

sections.title: World models are a different medium
sections.summary: He distinguishes Nereu from world-model-based game generation, calling world models a different medium with unsolved challenges including real-time 4K 60fps rendering and physics simulation, though he finds the space exciting.

sections.title: Closing and waitlist
sections.summary: Arturo invites the audience to join the waitlist, reflects that he is having fun making games again after 20 years in the industry and a period of disappointment, and takes questions outside.

organization.name: Nereu
organization.summary: Nereu is an independent AI-native game-creation company founded by Arturo Nunez. Its first-party site at nereu.co publishes an invite-only browser editor, templates such as Kart Rush and Skybound, and the Bibi assistant. Official instructions and the live Parts Catalog document the Asset Tag System: tags invite engine systems in, and tag config tunes them, so creators describe game intent instead of wiring traditional engine components. The product remains closed / invite-only while the creation experience is finished.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage, welcome instructions, Parts Catalog, and editor are live on nereu.co. Access is invite-only with a public waitlist. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
